newsitem.title: UK: PSBR still warrants UK fiscal tightening - analysts.
newsitem.headline: PSBR still warrants UK fiscal tightening - analysts.

text.p: UK fiscal policy still needs to be tightened, despite an unexpected budget surplus in April, if the new Labour government wants the public finances to return to balance, analysts said on Monday.
The UK posted a public sector surplus of 36 million stg in April, the first month of the 1997-98 financial year, defying predictions of a 1.7 billion public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR.)
"With the PSBR still uncomfortably high given the stage of the economic cycle, these numbers do not eradicate the need for a fiscal tightening," said HSBC economist Jonathan Loynes.
He argued that without a tighter fiscal stance, the country could not hope to return its finances to balance on a sustainable basis.

The Office for National Statistics also announced the deficit for fiscal 1996-97 had been revised up to 27.55 billion stg, excluding privatisation receipts from 27.24 billion. In 1995-96, it was 34.12 billion stg.
"The PSBR excluding privatisation proceeds for last year was around 3.5 percent of GDP and that is still too high." said Royal Bank of Scotland economist Marian Bell.
"Whether they need to do any more depends on whether the existing spending plans are met," she said.

New Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown has pledged to stick to the plans for public spending growth of just 2.0 percent over the next two months, laid out by Kenneth Clarke, Chancellor under the ousted Conservative government.

Bell said that if the new Labour government considered they were likely to be slightly adrift on such stringent spending plans then Brown might opt to raise an additional 2.0 to 5.0 billion stg in the budget expected in the next couple of months -- June 10 is the rumoured date.

"But I don't think it's likely to be more than that, it would be against the spirit of the election campaign -- that they weren't going to hammer the personal sector on taxes -- even if it isn't against the letter," she said.

HSBC's Loynes expects the budget too deliver a fiscal tightening of around 4.0 billion stg in addition to any money raised from the so-called windfall tax on privatised utilities, the revenue from which will be spent on the welfare-to-work scheme. This should ensure a PSBR of just 12.0 billion stg for this year, he said.
But Dresdner Kleinwort Benson economist David Owen argues that expectations of tightening are overdone. "I think there will be less in the way of tax rises than the market is expecting."
"Today's figures will keep Gordon Brown relatively confortable in the view that he doesn't have to aggressively raise taxes to fill some black hole in spending," he said.

Owen argues that the government is unlikely to miss the spending ceiling by as much as some commentators are suggesting: "They'll overrun but probably still have the percentage of deficit to GDP falling and in terms of the structural deficit, that's all they'll need to do."

The official forecast is for a PSBR of around 19.2 billion for the current fiscal year but significant downward revision to the Treasury's forecast in the budget, according to NatWest Markets economist John O'Sullivan.

The April data were flattered by proceeds of 700 million each from the sales of Ministry of Defence married quarters and the housing corporation's loan book as well as by the concentration of VAT receipts in the first month of the quarter.
But even so, the numbers are encouraging. "The rise in central goverment spending was modest and a good portent for the rest of the financial year," O'Sullivan said.
The data also showed receipts from employment taxes were up, after strong employment growth in the first quarter.

The UK Treasury were quick to try to dampen a surge in bullishness about the prospects for government borrowing this year. "One should not read too much into one month's figures at the start of the financial year," a spokesman said.
There is also a danger that the figures may further inflame the Bank of England's desire to exercise its new power to choose the level of interes rates.
The data however, may add to Bank of England worries that growth is too strong and to this end, they are not good news for the short end of the curve," Bank of America economist Jeremy Hawkins said.
